Advantages

  • Aesthetic aspect
  • Socio-professional reinsertion
  • Increased intraoperative visibility
  • Reduced immunology and metabolic reaction
  • Reduction of need of analgesics
  • Early mobilization
  • Reduction of postoperative ileus
  • Reduction or absence of parietal complications (immediate, early and late)
  • Reduction of intraperitoneal adhesions
  • Reduction of hospitalization period

Basic techniques in laparoscopic surgery

  • 1. Operative setting
  • Elective NOT emergency!
  • Skin shaved and disinfection (betadine or alcohol)
  • Thrombosis prophylaxis with elastic bandages and LMWH
  • Depending on type of surgery nasogastric, urinary catheter are inserted
  • AB prophylaxis
  • General anesthesia is mandatory to ensure proper relaxation of abdominal wall
  • 2. Induction of pneumoperitoneum
  • Usually made in umbilical point and Veress needle inserted
  • By blowing 3-6 l of CO2 through inflator
  • 3. Isobar chamber
  • In some situations, it is necessary to create isobaric pneumoperitoneum (ventricular-peritoneal drainage)
  • Achieved by suspending abdominal wall using special laparo-lifts
  • 4. Introduction of trocars
  • 1st 10 mm trocar inserted at umbilical site
  • Then laparoscope inserted and peritoneal cavity viewed
  • Under endoscopic control rest of trocars are inserted
  • 5. Diagnostic laparoscopy

= mandatory procedure at beginning of each intervention → detection of iatrogenic injury, surgical diseases or evaluate operability of case

  • 6. Laparoscopic dissection
  • Follows same basic principles as in open surgery
  • Can perform blunt or sharp dissections
  • 7. Hemostasis, laparoscopic suture ligatures
  • Mostly by electrocoagulation or clips
  • There are situations where it is necessary to perform hemostatic suture or ligature
  • New laparoscopic devices (LigaSure) perform coagulation and section
  • Vascular staplers can accomplish same thing
  • 8. Complications
  • Blowing into pro-peritoneal space
  • Injuring abdominal viscera
  • Pneumo-omentum
  • Gas embolism
  • Respiratory and cardiovascular complications
  • + specific complications of each type of surgery
  • 9. Conversion to open surgery
  • Indicated when occurrence of complications that cannot be solved through laparoscopic way, presence of

conditions that require open surgery or if surgery laparoscopic lasts well beyond standard duration and progression procedure is very slow

Modern improvements

  • NOTES surgery (Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery) - no scar surgery → natural body orifice
  • Robotic surgery - perform fine movements in confined spaces, increased precision, speed during surgery
  • Telesurgery - remotely perform entire surgery using robot coordinated from one console
  • Augmented reality - superimpose real image of operative field (classic or laparoscopic) with three- dimensional images reconstructed by computer tomography

book.html:
Laparoscopic surgery – general principles

Florin Graur, Radu Elisei

INTRODUCTION

Laparoscopic surgery begins in 1901 when George Kelling makes first peritoneal cavity examination with a cystoscope. Semm set up in 1944 an automatic insufflation system with various tools adapted to this method (trocars, scissors, clips applicator and graspers). Same author performed in 1983 the first laparoscopic appendectomy. The real momentum of laparoscopic surgery appears in 1990 when laparoscopic cholecystectomy became the gold standard. Subsequently other techniques were developed and conventional surgical procedures were transferred in laparoscopic surgery. In addition it begins the foundation of telesurgery and robotic surgery.

The principles of classical surgery are respected in laparoscopic surgery, except that the used devices are different. Any surgeon practicing laparoscopic techniques must first be master of the classical techniques, which may be required when intervention cannot go through laparoscopic technique.

The training that a general surgeon needs to acquire skills and knowledge necessary for laparoscopic surgery includes several stages: theoretical stage, simulator exercises and participation in the experimental stage surgery with experienced surgeons.

For the simulator stage there is currently a lot of simulators that allow students to practice the simple procedures like knots, sutures, etc., to complex procedures such as liver or colon resections.

The advantages of laparoscopic surgery are: aesthetic aspect, socioprofessional reinsertion, increased intraoperative visibility, reduced immunology and metabolic reaction, reduction of the need of analgesics, early mobilization, reduction of postoperative ileus, reduction or absence of parietal complications (immediate, early and late), reduction of intraperitoneal adhesions, reduction of hospitalization period.

DEVICES AND INSTRUMENTS

To achieve laparoscopic surgery it is needed to create a pneumoperitoneum, i.e. blowing gas into the peritoneal cavity. To do so, 3-6 liters of CO . Pneumoperioneum is done by inserting a needle (Veress needle)

2 into the peritoneal cavity through an incision of the skin usually performed at umbilicus. After creating pneumoperitoneum (a "workroom" situated between the anterior abdominal wall and abdominal organs), a 5 or 10 mm diameter trocar is inserted to be used for the laparoscope. A laparoscope connected to a video camera is inserted through the trocar and the image of the intra-abdominal organs appears on the monitor. Under visual control trocars are further inserted, in positions and numbers that vary depending on the needs. Trocars are designed to keep the gas inside the peritoneal cavity, thus keeping the workroom. One of the trocars is connected to the insufflator that maintains workroom in gas losses, by blowing heated gas until a pressure between 12 and 14 mm Hg. Over this pressure gas will not be instilled into the peritoneal cavity, thus avoiding barotrauma.

Apart from insufflation system there are several systems: wash-suction system, video system, electrosurgical system. The wash-suction module comprises a pump that propels saline at body temperature via a cannula into the peritoneal cavity and another module which suction the washing liquid in the external collecting vessel. Video circuit is composed of a laparoscope (a rigid instrument 5 or 10 mm diameter containing optical fibers, prisms and lenses that transmit the image outside the abdominal cavity) connected to a camera that transforms the image into electrical signal. This electrical signal is converted by a video processing module into an image on the monitor where the surgeon look at the procedure. Another module is cold light source, which, through an optical cable transmits light to the laparoscope and through it, in the peritoneal cavity. The used laparoscopes may from 0, 30 to 45 degrees, and more recently have flexible tip, that allows the operator to obtain images of the peritoneal cavity from different angles. In addition there are variants of laparoscopes that provides three-dimensional images using two cameras. Video systems have photo and video recording devices and the procedure could be remotely transmitted. The electrosurgery system may work in monopolar or in bipolar mode. Monopolar mode closes the electrical circuit between the active electrode pole (usually hook electrode) and passive electrode (grounding plate) through the patient tissues, thermal effect being achieved at the tip of the active electrode pole. Bipolar module closes the electrical circuit between bipolar electrodes without passing electrical energy through other areas of the patient's body.

All these devices are placed in the operating room on a winch specifically designed to minimize the space occupied by all this equipment.

A number of trocars have been imagined for the access of laparoscopic surgery devices inside the abdominal cavity. Their diameters ranging from 3 mm to 5 mm (for the introduction of forceps or mini-laparoscopes), up to 10-12 or 15 mm laparoscope, Ligasure clamps or linear staplers. Trocars position and diameter varies depending on the intervention proposed and the type of devices used. For each type of surgery there is one or more preferred position depending on the school of surgery or surgeon preferences.

Dissecting, gripping or extraction forceps have shapes and diameters varying depending on their usefulness. Their diameter varies from 3 to 5 or 10 mm. The surgeon will select the graspers to get enough traction to be achieved in tissue dissection, but also to avoid perforation of organs because of very sharply graspers or with very big teeth. Some graspers can be coupled to electrocoagulation system.

Laparoscopic scissors have diverse shapes, mostly having diameter of 5 mm. Some scissors can be coupled to the electrosurgical system.

Laparoscopic needle holders are made for intracorporeal sutures. They generally have a diameter of 5 mm and except the suture, they are used to perform intracorporeal knot.

A faster way for ligation are metal clips applied using laparoscopic applicators. These are of two types: reusable applicators, to be reloaded after each clip applied, and the disposable automatic clippers containing 15-20 sets that can be applied without extracting the device outside the operating field. Theclips are made of metal, plastic or absorbable material.

Other instruments used in laparoscopic surgery are the fan-type retractor and extraction basket. In recent years were introduced in laparoscopic surgery various other items such as ultrasound dissection systems (ultrasonic scalpel), blood vessel sealing systems, circular or linear staplers, etc. Ultrasonic scalpel acts by tissue dissection and coagulation using an electrode that produces high intensity ultrasounds that are converted into heat at the point of action. Blood vessels sealing systems like Ligasure seals the vessel on both sides then section it after completing coagulation. Argon beam performs coagulation on surface areas with diffuse bleeding. Intraoperative laparoscopic ultrasound can be performed using special transducers, which are inserted through the trocars of 10 mm. Choledocoscopes are useful in cases in which the surgeon intends to examine the contents of the common bile duct or intrahepatic bile channels. Also during these maneuvers, where stones are identified, they can be extracted using basket (Dormia) or Fogarty probes. Lithotripsy is useful for large stones that cannot be extracted without prior crushing in bile duct lumen.

BASIC TECHNIQUES IN LAPAROSCOPIC SURGERY

Operative setting

In order to perform laparoscopic surgery, the abdominal wall skin should be shaved, and for scheduled operations (not in emergency) it is recommended to avoid intervention if there are skin infections. The skin is disinfected with antiseptic solutions (Betadine or alcohol).

For prophylaxis of deep vein thrombosis elastic bandages are recommended to be put on the calves and in the day before surgery low molecular weight heparins should be administered.

Depending on the type of surgery, naso-gastric tube or bladder tube should be inserted. Also in operations with septic potential, prophylactic antibiotic treatment is given.

General anesthesia is mandatory for laparoscopic surgery to ensure proper relaxation of the abdominal wall.

Position of the team varies depending on the type of surgery proposed. The cameraman directs the laparoscope into the operative field and usually it sits on the same side of the patient as the operator, with a monitor directly accessible in the visual field. Depending on the needs, the team may be supplemented by one or two assistants who will maintain organs in position using graspers.

The induction of pneumoperitoneum

Usually inducing pneumoperitoneum is made in the umbilical point. The skin is raised at the cranial pole of the umbilicus and a vertical or transverse incision of approximately 10 mm is performed. The Veress needle is inserted into the peritoneum. The proper introduction is checked through various tests. Subsequently Veress needle is connected to an insufflator and a 12 mm Hg pressure is made (by blowing it 3-6 l of CO ).

2

Isobar chamber

In some situations it is necessary to create an isobaric pneumoperitoneum (patients with ventricular-peritoneal drainage, etc). This is achieved by suspending the abdominal wall using special laparolifts.

The introduction of trocars

The first 10 mm trocar is inserted at umbilical site, raising the clamps applied to the skin. Then the laparoscope is inserted and the peritoneal cavity is viewed. Under endoscopic control the rest of the trocars are inserted, number and position will vary according to the needs of the operator and the type of surgery proposed.

Diagnostic laparoscopy

Diagnostic laparoscopy is a mandatory procedure at the beginning of each intervention being that maneuver during which the peritoneal cavity is explored for the detection of iatrogenic injury, surgical diseases or to evaluate the operability of the case.

Laparoscopic dissection

Laparoscopic dissection follows the same basic principles as in open surgery. It can perform blunt dissection (pad mounted or suction cannula) or sharp (electrode cautery or scissors).

Haemostasis, laparoscopic suture ligatures and

Hemostasis in laparoscopic surgery is done most easily by electrocoagulation or with clips. However there are situations where it is necessary to perform hemostatic suture or ligature. The new laparoscopic devices (LigaSure) performs coagulation and section, thus easing the work of the surgeon. The vascular staplers can accomplish the same thing by applying special staples.

Complications of laparoscopic surgery

Among the complications of laparoscopic surgery are the following: blowing into the properitoneal space, injuring the abdominal viscera, pneumo-omentum, gas embolism, respiratory and cardiovascular complications, plus specific complications of each type of surgery.

Conversion to open surgery

Conversion to an open intervention is indicated when the surgeon finds the occurrence of complications that cannot be solved through laparoscopic way, presence of conditions that require open surgery or if surgery laparoscopic lasts well beyond the standard duration and progression procedure is very slow.

Modern Trends

A number of improvements have been made in recent years in laparoscopic procedures including: NOTES surgery, robotic surgery, telesurgery, augmented reality, etc.

Surgery NOTES (Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery) surgery is "no scar surgery". This approach is achieved through the body's natural orifices (mouth, anus, vagina) or embryological approach E-NOTES (Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic embryologic-surgery) is done through umbilicus. For this surgery there were designed special tools and interventions are made by combining these tools with interventional endoscopes.

Robotic surgery performes various surgeries using medical robots that have the ability to reduce surgeon’s tremor, to perform fine movements in confined spaces and increased precision and speed during surgery. Of course, these robots and consumables costs increase the total cost of surgery.

Telesurgery is the manner by which a surgeon can remotely perform the entire surgery using a robot coordinated from one console. The first such operation (Operation Lindbergh) was made by Professor J. Marescaux from Strasbourg (France) who performed a cholecystectomy from New York to a patient in Strasbourg with a Zeus-type robot in 2001.

Augmented reality superimpose the real image of the operative field (classic or laparoscopic) with three-dimensional images reconstructed by computer tomography of the patient, thus providing further details for surgeon to identify more precisely the position of tumors, anatomical malformations or intra-parenchymal vital structures.
